**Warning threshold:** a 15‑minute demand of **1,125 kW** (90 % of the contract) or a ≥ 20 % probability of exceeding the contract in the next hour.  

- The plant’s contract capacity is **1,250 kW** (see [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Demand status tiers]).  
- The warning level is defined as **90 % of the contract**, i.e. **1,125 kW** (see [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Demand status tiers]).  

A warning is raised when the projected 15‑minute demand reaches or exceeds this 1,125 kW level **or** when the model predicts a ≥ 20 % chance that the next‑hour demand will surpass the 1,250 kW contract. This early‑warning point gives operators time to shed or shift loads before the demand crosses the contract limit and incurs the higher exceedance charges (2× the contract price up to 10 % over, 3× beyond that).

**Billing of demand that exceeds the contract capacity**

- The plant’s contracted capacity is **1,250 kW** (regular contract).  
- For each 15‑minute interval where the measured demand is **above 1,250 kW**, the excess kW are charged at the period’s contract price **× 2** up to **10 % over the contract** (i.e., up to **1,375 kW**).  
- Any demand **beyond 1,375 kW** is charged at **× 3** the contract price.  

[unverified citation removed]  
[unverified citation removed]

The night‑load baseline uses a **CUSUM allowance k = 0.5** and an **alarm threshold h = 8 (in robust sigmas)**. An alarm also requires the night‑load to be more than **3 kW above expectation**【source: docs/anomaly_detection.md#Anomaly detection > Layer 2: baseline drift (`anomaly/baseline.py`)】.

The load‑forecaster predicts the **change from an anchor** rather than the absolute demand level because:

- Tree‑based models (LightGBM quantile models) cannot forecast values that exceed anything seen during training.  
- In the plant’s historical data the contract was rarely exceeded, so a “level‑target” model never warned about an exceedance – the first version missed all exceedances.  
- By predicting a **change** (increment) on top of the current load (the anchor), the model can add heat‑driven or start‑up‑driven steps without needing to exceed any training‑seen value.  

The anchor is the last completed interval for short horizons (15 min–3 h) and the same time last week for day‑ahead forecasts. Two refinements keep the prediction bands honest: quantile crossing (P10 ≤ P50 ≤ P90) and conformal widening, which scales the band so that 80 % of held‑out days fall inside P10‑P90.  

[source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

**Weekday peak‑period hours (summer, 16 May – 15 October):** 16:00 – 22:00 (local time, Asia/Taipei)  

- Price during this period: **NT$9.39 /kWh**  
- Source: [docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-03_tariff_guide.md#EM-03 Tariff Guide > Time-of-use periods and energy prices > Summer (16 May - 15 October)]

**What operators should do on a very hot afternoon when the forecast warns that demand may exceed the contract**

1. **Check the forecast and trigger the procedure**  
   - If the one‑hour forecast gives **P(exceed) ≥ 20 % (WARNING)** or **P(exceed) ≥ 50 % (ALARM)**, start the heat‑wave pre‑cooling procedure (SOP‑06).  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

2. **Pre‑cooling preparation (Step 1 of SOP‑06)**  
   - Confirm the outdoor‑temperature forecast with the energy coordinator.  
   - Make sure condensers and the cooling‑tower are clean (EQ‑07, EQ‑08).  
   - Verify that both chillers are available and set in lead/lag order, with **CH‑01 as lead**.  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

3. **EV‑charging pause readiness (Step 4 of SOP‑06)**  
   - Confirm the EV‑01 pause function works.  
   - Warn staff at the EV bank that charging may be paused.  
   - **Pause EV charging as soon as a WARNING appears** – the 28 kW EV load can be shed without affecting production.  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

4. **Compressed‑air system check (Step 5 of SOP‑06)**  
   - Check compressor intake temperature and filters.  
   - Be ready to **lower the compressed‑air pressure by 0.5 bar** (≈ 3.5 % of present compressor load) if needed.  
   - Fix any known leaks first (SOP‑04).  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

5. **During the peak window (Step 6 of SOP‑06)**  
   - **Monitor projected demand every 15‑minute interval.**  
   - If a WARNING or ALARM is raised, **follow SOP‑03 (Demand‑Exceedance Response)** and shed loads in the play‑book order.  
   - **Raise the chilled‑water setpoint by +1 °C** (≈ 4 % of the present chiller load) **if the pre‑cooling margin allows**.  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

6. **Never shed critical loads**  
   - Do **not** shed the server room, injection molders that are mid‑cycle, or reflow ovens with boards inside.  
   - [unverified citation removed]  

**Summary:**  
When a hot‑afternoon forecast raises a WARNING or ALARM, operators start SOP‑06, clean and ready the chillers, pause EV charging, adjust compressor pressure, monitor demand continuously, and, if necessary, shed non‑critical loads per SOP‑03 while protecting essential production equipment.

**16 June 2025 start‑up incident (scenario S2)**  

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Peak demand** | **1324.4 kW** at **2025‑06‑16 08:15** | [data: get_demand] |
| **Contract capacity** | 1250 kW | [data: get_plant_overview] |
| **Exceedance** | 6 % above contract (1324.4 / 1250 = 1.06) | [data: get_demand] |
| **Cause** | Simultaneous start‑up of many machines on Monday morning (scenario S2). Reflow ovens, injection molders, compressors and other loads all began within the same 15‑minute interval, pushing demand well over the contract. | [source: docs/scenarios.md#Scenario engine > Event types] |
| **Effect of a 15‑minute stagger** | Peak would drop to **1141.5 kW** (reduction of **182.9 kW**). The plant would stay **below** the contract, avoiding the exceedance penalty. | [data: whatif_staggered_start] |
| **Penalty avoided** | **NT$6,652** (≈ US$208) | [data: whatif_staggered_start] |

**What a 15‑minute stagger would have achieved**

- Peak demand reduced from 1324.4 kW to **1141.5 kW** – a drop of **182.9 kW** (≈ 13.8 % lower).  
- The plant would have remained **under the 1250 kW contract**, so no contract‑exceedance warning or alarm would have been triggered.  
- The **NT$6,652 exceedance penalty** (US$208) would have been avoided.  

In practice, staggering the start‑up of high‑power equipment (e.g., reflow ovens, injection molders, air compressors) by just 15 minutes spreads the inrush current over time, keeping the 15‑minute demand peak well within the contracted limit.

**What happened**

- From 2025‑11‑03 to 2025‑11‑12 the capacitor bank on **MDB‑3 tripped** (incident S8).  
  The board’s power factor dropped from its normal **0.96** down to **0.84** [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Reference case: incident S8].

- On **5 Nov 2025** (08:00‑17:00) the daytime average power factor for MDB‑3 was **0.849** (minimum 0.845, maximum 0.852) [data: get_meter_series].

**Maintenance check**

- The tripped capacitor bank is the root cause.  
- Follow **SOP‑05** “Power Factor Check”:  
  1. Verify the board’s 15‑minute average PF is rising back toward the normal ~0.96.  
  2. Confirm the low‑power‑factor rule clears.  
  3. Record the days the bank was out and restore/replace the capacitor bank as needed.  

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 4: verify]
